Rand Locked

By: Bernadette Maguire | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The rand is plummeting - what does it mean for travel and how and where can you get the most bang for your buck.

Summary:
Travel is widely acknowledged as critical to shaping our world view - giving us an education.

But now more and more SA's are being rand locked.

The only affordable options left is: India, Vietnam, Thailand and Bali.

We take a look at what water and coffee and travel will cost you using well known brand and benchmarks.

For instance: A burger from Nandos will cost you R36 here but R286 rand in London. bottle of water R4 in Bail, R8 in SA and R52 in London.

We show you just how the rand has impacted

Press Release:


Randlocked
Would you pay R280 for a burger? It may sound outrageous, but if you are a South African travelling through London, this is how much a Nando’s burger would set you back right now. How about an entrance ticket for entry to a German museum at a cool R510? The Rand has plummeted to all-time lows against international currencies, leaving South Africans stranded at home. Has international travel become near impossible for rand-locked South African travellers, or can you still get some bang for your buck in India, Thailand or Bali? Carte Blanche explores your options.


Script:


Script Rand locked


VO: 11
Travel, they say is one of the best ways to broaden you mind. Exploration a critical part of our education believes the doyenne of travel journalism –Kate Turkington.

Kate:
Travel is one of the most important things anybody can do because why? Because you educate yourself, you learn about other people, you find out that other people are exactly the same as you, you find out that other places are wonderful and beautiful but that we still have some of the most wonderful and beautiful places right here in South Africa.

VO: 12
But over the past few weeks South Africans have watched in horror as the liquid rand went into free fall – its put travel out of reach for most South Africans says economist Xanthi Payi.

Derek:
So what do we do if we want to see the world?

Xanthi:
Watch your TV, that might help you a little bit more, The Discovery channel.

Derek:
When we try to find the villain behind the falling rand we may think of the El Nene storm in December but the causes actually go way beyond that.

VO: 11
Although our internal politics and the drought are affecting the currency so are external factors – like the impact of the slowing down of the Chinese economy saw the rand hitting new lows says economist Advocate Lavan Gopaul

Lavan:
A slowdown in Chinese growth saw data out this week that pointed to a smaller Chinese economy. It hurt global markets and in particular the South Africa rand was a casualty.

Xanthi:
China itself is worried about their own growth because it seems to be slowing more than expected so they are trying to manipulate their currency to make exports cheaper.

VO: 3”
So what’s the rand really worth?

Derek:
It’s Wednesday the 13th of January at 10 in the morning because this rand does seem to move around a bit. Let’s see what we have to play with. Let’s look at the rand dollar exchange rate.

VO:
We did the maths and looked at what your rand is worth in dollar terms.

Derek:
There you have it 0,060 dollars. So for every rand you are getting 6 American cents.

VO: 17”
Buy in Euros and its even worse – about 5,7cents and you’ll get 4.2 pence for your rand in the UK. Xanthi says he thought he’d been given the wrong bill when he ordered a G and T in New York recently.

Xanthi:
R350 for a gin and tonic. And then I thought I’d downgrade to beer and then you pay about R120 for a beer.

VO: 6”
We decided to do our own price index using menus from Nando’s on the internet.

Derek upsound: burger and water…that’s all.

VO: 40”
This is what we found:

In South Africa you’ll pay R34,90 for a burger and R14 for a 500ml bottle of water. That’s R48,90.

In London it will set you back: R195,44.

In the US you’ll have to fork out R185.

And in Singapore a whopping R261,49.

VO: 1-“
Johnathan and Georgie Wagner experienced the impact first hand. They visited family in Germany. Just days before they left finance minister Nene was sacked.

Johnathan :
In 48 hours my money that I had allocated was devalued by R3000.

VO: 7”
And the holiday which just a few years ago cost R40 000 had almost doubled in price. Everything was more expensive.

Johnathan:
We looked at going to the museum in Munich. The museum in Munich was 35 euros for an adult, 16 euros for a child and you look at that and you think to yourself wow that’s a 100 euros. Just to get in.

VO: 6
That’s just over R1700 rand.
And a few rounds of drinks with a relative?

Johnathan:
It cost us in the region of about R2500 just for 4 drinks each.

VO: 2”
Fancy a cuppa?

Georgie:
Tea no milk, no sugar just tea, 50 bucks.

VO: 3”
And two glasses of water at the local theatre?

Georgie:
Not even sparkling, not even bubbles and it was 7 euros – it worked out at R120. I told my kids they had to finish every last drop boy.

VO: 11”
Students Mikayla Maher and Matt Bowden were in for some eye openers on their trip to South East Asia too. Their first stop on route – Doha airport.

Matt:
We ordered a coffee for R80 and then Mikayla ordered a yoghurt for R140.

VO: 3”
Singapore was no different.

Mikayla:
Matt ordered a milkshake for R180 and that filled him up for the day - one milkshake.

VO: 4
On Christmas eve that went out for a humble dinner.

Matt:
We ordered a burger and a coke and the bill was R350 each.

Mikayala:
For a burger and a coke. I felt trapped in Singapore, because it was so amazing and so beautiful but I just felt that we couldn’t do anything.

Derek:

VO: 4”
Accomodation in these big cities isn’t cheap either.

Derek upsound:
Let’s try something different I am looking for 4 star hotels again around the world – an equivalent hotel group.

VO: 22”
Hilton New York comes in at 129USD – so still affordable at R2134

London rate 199 pounds – that’s – R4744

Singapore 276 dollars – so R4567

Derek link:
So if we are pretty much randlocked are there still some international options for those who have the travel bug?

Lavan:
There are opportunities for inexpensive travel particularly in Asia Vietnam, India, Indonesia may be destinations to consider as well as Turkey.

VO: 6”
Mikayla and Matt visited Thailand as well on their trip and they said it was like chalk and cheese.

Mikayla:
It was amazing, it was cheap for us – you really felt that you could afford it.


VO: 4
Dinner and a drink in Thailand cost 60 bucks.

Derek:
So you’re saying that travelling around Thailand, Malaysia may be cheaper than a local holiday?

Mikayla:
Day to day…definitely.

VO: 7”
Travel writer Brendan Seery believes we might as well write off the iconic destinations.

Brendan:
If you can find self catering apartments in London, you can look at air bnb as well, you can do a house swop those are all ways of saving money.


VO:
In the current climate packages and cruises may be the way to go.

Brendan:
Things like offshore cruises from here, like the MSC cruises from Durban, what I call the booze cruise, its so popular with people because its cheap, its affordable and it gives you the impression of being on an overseas trip, even if you aren’t really, you’re just pottering around the Indian Ocean or maybe going to Madagascar.

VO: 10”
There are also some very creative and cheap travel alternatives. Donovan Risk and a few friends visited Vietnam during December – they toured the country on motorbikes.

Don:
We rented a bike for 6 days – it cost us roughly R1500. If you wanted to buy a bike it would cost R3000 and you could easily sell it.

VO: 4”
They stayed in backpackers along most of their route.

Don:
It ranged from R80 to R120 and some of them included breakfast in that price.

VO: 9”
Most of their meals cost between R20 and R30 rand and he couldn’t believe how little a beer sold for in some of the villages.

Don:
But then you get the odd places where especially outside the tourist destinations it can go down toR3 a beer easily.

Derek:
It’s not a local brew?

Don:
It’s local from the actual manufacturers its not something someone brewed in their back yard or anything like that.

VO:
So a two week holiday including his R7000 airfare cost him R17 000.

Derek
It’s not easy to find an economist who predicts a rosy financial future for the country but we are left with the burning question can the exchange rate and our travel opportunities improve?

Xanthi
It’s very, very serious situation – things that we are looking out now suggests that we are facing more weakness rather than strength.

Georgie:
It’s actually sad that the average normal middle class citizen can’t afford.

Johnathan:
I think South Africans are going to be those people who have their faces pressed up against the glass, looking in from the outside because can’t afford to go in anywhere.

VO: 8”
The only upside is that local tourism will be stimulated as more people choose to explore our own backyard.

Kate:
But good things can happen because now we can discover out own country.

VO: 4
And there’s evidence that South Africans are doing just that.

Kate:
Tourism figures are up, even in spite of the Visa qualifications – I think they were up 7% in December.

VO: 3”
And of course there’s our neighbouring states.

Brendan:
Absolutely, if you have never been to Namibia you have got to go, I think Zimbabwe is a slumbering giant, Mozambique can be cheap, Botswana is good but Botswana is expensive as well. So basically what did Satour used to say – we have a world in our own country - travel at home.

VO: 9”
So while our options are limited it doesn’t mean that we can’t still explore.

Mikayla:
I want to go back to Thailand or Bali because I loved it so much. There is so much to explore actually. I feel I didn’t do enough of it.

VO: 8”
And Don’s already planning his next overseas adventure in Gautemala and Costa Rica where he wants to go volcano boarding.

Don
Where you literally have a board like snowboarding but down a volcano and interesting stuff like that. So you just have to think of the places that might bee popular in 5 or 10 years and jump onto those places before they get too popular.

Promo 1:

VO: 7”
Can South Africans still afford to travel to our iconic overseas destinations or are they fast slipping out of reach?

Johnathan:
SA’s are going to be those people with their faces pressed up against the window.


VO: 8”
We meet a young man who bucked the currency blues and found a way to travel overseas on a budget of R300 a day.

Don:
End comment …. before they get too popular


VO: 10”
R180 for a milkshake, R70 for a glass of water and R350 for a burger and soda – the battered rand is putting international travel way out of reach for most South Africans.
